The Battle of Hastings. On the fourteenth of October, ten sixty-six, one of history's most consequential battles was fought near Hastings in East Sussex. After King Edward the Confessor's death, the English throne was disputed. William the Conqueror, Duke of Normandy, claimed that Edward had promised him the crown. Harold Godwinson, the Anglo-Saxon noble, claimed it for himself. They decided the matter by combat, with seven thousand Norman troops crossing from Normandy to invade England.

The Norman forces were outnumbered, but they possessed superior tactics. Their cavalry charges and archers in disciplined formation proved devastatingly effective against the Saxon defensive shield-wall. Harold Godwinson died in the battle—accounts say he took an arrow to the eye, a symbolic end to the Anglo-Saxon age. With his death, resistance collapsed. William claimed the throne as King William I, and the Norman Conquest of England was complete.

The victory reshaped England itself. Norman rule lasted for centuries, fundamentally transforming English institutions, law, and language with French-Norman influence. English would absorb thousands of Norman French words. The feudal system was restructured according to Norman principles. The victory is immortalised in the Bayeux Tapestry, an eleventh-century embroidered narrative that depicts the invasion and the battle itself, one of history's most remarkable historical documents. The Battle of Hastings marks a threshold—the moment when Anglo-Saxon England yielded to Norman and French cultural dominance.
